title: Your First Steps
learningGoals: Know some common early signs of pregnancy, and that every pregnancy is different
Know why starting prenatal care early matters and when it is best to start
Know how much folic acid public-health guidance recommends each day, and why
Check with your care team before starting or stopping any medicine
Know simple ways to ease nausea and the signs of dehydration that mean you should call

review.notes: Clinically reviewed 2026-10-17 by Bryan Kurtz MD, FACOG; every source confirmed against its slides. Rebuilt 2026-10-15 from the earlier published Early Pregnancy Basics course. The old course's dehydration list included 'unable to urinate', which the ACOG page does not list; it now follows ACOG's three signs plus not keeping food or fluids down.

slides.heading: Your First Steps
onScreen: Early Pregnancy Basics · Lesson 1
About 8 minutes
slides.narration: Welcome to Early Pregnancy Basics. I'm so glad you're here. Finding out you're pregnant can bring a lot of feelings at once. Excitement, worry, and plenty of questions. All of that is normal. In this first lesson, we'll talk about what early pregnancy can feel like, why it helps to start prenatal care early, a vitamin called folic acid, and some simple ways to handle nausea. This class is general information. Your own care team will help you make a plan that fits you. Let's get started.

visual.description: Calm, hopeful scene of a person sitting at a kitchen table with a cup of tea, smiling softly at a phone, with a partner resting a hand on their shoulder. Diverse people, soft peach and sage colors.

slides.heading: What early pregnancy can feel like
onScreen: A missed period is often the first sign
Tender breasts, tiredness, and nausea are common
Peeing more often and mood swings, too
Every pregnancy is different
slides.narration: For many people, the first sign of pregnancy is a missed period. Your body may give you other signs, too. Your breasts may feel sore, full, or tingly. You may feel more tired than usual. Many people feel queasy, and this can happen at any time of day, not just in the morning. You might need to pee more often, notice new food cravings, or go off foods you used to love. Your moods may swing more than usual. That's your hormones at work. Some people have lots of these signs, and some have very few. Both are normal.

visual.description: Soft pastel icons in a row: a calendar with a circled date, a sleepy face, a glass of water, a heart with a small wave for mood. Gentle lavender and cream palette.

slides.heading: Start prenatal care early
onScreen: Prenatal care is health care during pregnancy
Best to start in the first trimester
Before 10 weeks after your last period is ideal
Starting later? Call now. It's not too late.
slides.narration: Prenatal care is simply health care for you while you're pregnant. Getting early and regular care can help your care team spot problems sooner and help manage them. It's best to start in the first trimester, which is the first three months of pregnancy. Ideally, that's before ten weeks after the first day of your last period. But life happens. Maybe you just found out, or it's taking time to find someone near you. If you're starting later than you hoped, that's okay. Call now, and your care team will help you take the next steps.

visual.description: Simple soft-colored timeline of the first trimester, weeks one to thirteen, with a gentle highlight up to week ten labeled 'Ideal time to start care'.

slides.heading: Who can care for you
onScreen: Ob-gyns (pregnancy and women's health doctors)
Midwives
Family medicine doctors
Already have a doctor? Ask if they offer prenatal care
slides.narration: Several kinds of professionals can give prenatal care. Most people see an ob-gyn. That's a doctor who specializes in pregnancy and women's health. Midwives care for people with average-risk pregnancies, from early pregnancy through birth and after. Family medicine doctors can also care for average-risk pregnancies. If a health problem comes up, you might be referred to a specialist. If you already have a doctor, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner, ask if they offer prenatal care. And ask whether they can also help deliver your baby.

visual.description: Three friendly clinicians of different backgrounds standing side by side, one in scrubs, one in a midwife's cardigan, one in a white coat. Warm, soft colors.

slides.heading: Folic acid: a small step that matters
onScreen: 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid every day
Helps your baby's brain and spine form
Matters most in the first few weeks
Check vitamin and food labels for folic acid
slides.narration: Folic acid is a vitamin. The CDC recommends that anyone who could become pregnant get four hundred micrograms of folic acid every day. That's written as four hundred m c g on labels. Folic acid helps your baby's brain and spine form. Those parts start forming in the first few weeks of pregnancy, often before someone even knows they're pregnant. That's why it matters so much early on. You can get folic acid from a vitamin, and it's also added to some foods, like many breakfast cereals. Check the label to be sure. Some people need a different amount because of their health history, so ask your care team what's right for you.

visual.description: A vitamin bottle next to a bowl of cereal, leafy greens, beans, and an orange, with a small label callout reading '400 mcg folic acid'. Soft green and yellow tones.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: Let's pause for a quick check-in.

question.prompt: Why does folic acid matter so much early in pregnancy?
options: It helps your baby's brain and spine form, which starts in the first few weeks
It's only needed in the last few months
question.explanation: Folic acid helps the baby's brain and spine form, and that happens very early, often before people know they're pregnant. The CDC recommends four hundred micrograms a day. Ask your care team if you need a different amount.

slides.heading: Medicines and supplements
onScreen: Don't stop or start a medicine on your own
Talk with your care team first
List everything: prescriptions, over-the-counter, vitamins, herbs
slides.narration: Here's an important one. If you take any medicine, don't stop it or start a new one on your own just because you're pregnant. Talk with your care team first. Some health conditions need to stay well controlled during pregnancy, and your team can help you weigh your choices. Make a list of everything you take. That means prescriptions, medicines you buy without a prescription, vitamins, herbal products, and other supplements. You'll bring this list to your first visit.

visual.description: A person writing a list on a notepad beside a few pill bottles and a tea box, a phone showing a clinic contact nearby. Muted blue and cream palette.

slides.heading: Nausea is common
onScreen: Can happen any time of day
Usually starts before 9 weeks
For most, it eases by about 14 weeks
Talk to your team if it's affecting your life
slides.narration: Nausea and vomiting are very common in early pregnancy. People call it morning sickness, but it can happen at any time of day. It usually starts before nine weeks. For most people, it eases by about fourteen weeks, though for some it lasts longer. Nausea usually doesn't harm your baby. But it can make daily life hard, like going to work or taking care of your family. If it's affecting your life or worrying you, talk with your care team. There are safe ways to help, and it's better to get help early.

visual.description: A person resting on a couch with a blanket, a plate of crackers and a glass of water on a side table, morning light. Diverse, soft rose and cream colors.

slides.heading: Simple ways to ease nausea
onScreen: Small meals often, so your stomach is never empty
Dry crackers before you get out of bed
Sip fluids all through the day
Steer clear of smells that bother you
slides.narration: Let's look at a few simple things that may help. Watch this short demonstration.

video.brief: Instructor in a kitchen shows: keeping dry toast or crackers by the bed to eat before getting up; eating five or six mini meals a day; bland foods that stay down; sipping water throughout the day, not just when thirsty; using a fan while cooking and asking someone else to take out the trash. Closes with: 'Before trying any medicine or supplement for nausea, ask your care team what's right for you.' No doses or product names.

slides.heading: Signs of dehydration: call your care team
onScreen: Small amount of dark urine
Dizzy or faint when you stand up
Racing or pounding heartbeat
Can't keep food or fluids down, or losing weight
slides.narration: Vomiting can make your body lose fluids. If those fluids aren't replaced, you can become dehydrated. Call your care team if you notice any of these signs. You're only peeing a small amount, and it's dark in color. You feel dizzy or faint when you stand up. Or your heart is racing or pounding. Also call if you can't keep food or fluids down, or you're starting to lose weight. Severe nausea can be treated, and getting help early can keep it from getting worse.

slides.heading: Your next steps
onScreen: Who will you call to start prenatal care?
Folic acid: are you getting 400 mcg a day?
Start your list of medicines and supplements
slides.narration: Let's turn this into action. Think about who you'll call to start prenatal care, and when. Check whether you're getting four hundred micrograms of folic acid each day. And start your list of medicines, vitamins, and supplements. Write down your plan here. It saves to your Birth Readiness Brief, so you can bring it to your first visit.
slides.prompt: Who will you call to start prenatal care, and by when? List any medicines, vitamins, or supplements you take now.

visual.description: A hand checking off a simple three-item list on a phone screen, with a small vitamin bottle nearby. Soft teal and cream.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Early signs vary from person to person
Start prenatal care early, ideally before 10 weeks
400 mcg of folic acid every day
Check with your team before changing medicines
Nausea is common; dehydration means call
slides.narration: Great work. Let's recap. Early pregnancy feels different for everyone. Start prenatal care early. Before ten weeks after your last period is ideal, but if you're later, just call now. Get four hundred micrograms of folic acid every day. Don't start or stop medicines on your own. Talk to your care team first. And nausea is common, but signs of dehydration mean it's time to call. Next, a few review questions. In the next lesson, we'll look at more common changes and when to reach out.

reviewQuiz.prompt: When is the best time to start prenatal care?
options: In the first trimester, ideally before 10 weeks after your last period
Only after your belly starts to show
In the last three months of pregnancy
reviewQuiz.explanation: It's best to start in the first trimester, ideally before ten weeks after the first day of your last period. If you're starting later, call now. Your care team will help with next steps.

reviewQuiz.prompt: You take a prescription medicine and just learned you're pregnant. What should you do?
options: Keep taking it and never mention it
Talk with your care team before making any change
reviewQuiz.explanation: Don't start or stop a medicine on your own. Your care team can help you decide what's best for you and your pregnancy.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which of these is a sign of dehydration that means you should call your care team?
options: Feeling dizzy or faint when you stand up
Craving a food you didn't used to like
Feeling a little queasy before breakfast
reviewQuiz.explanation: Dizziness or fainting when you stand, a small amount of dark urine, or a racing heartbeat can be signs of dehydration. Call your care team if you notice them.
